why_how.text: Every applicant is vision-tested, so knowing the outcomes avoids surprises at the counter.

scenario.text: Tomas wears glasses and takes his vision test with them on.

reasoning.text: Testing while wearing corrective lenses puts a corrective lenses restriction on the license.

result.text: Tomas passes, and his license carries the corrective lenses restriction.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a failed vision test simply means trying again later at the counter.

correction.text: A failed vision test sends you to an eye doctor for a completed Report of Vision Examination form.

memory_support.text: Lenses on, restriction on; fail it, see the eye doctor.

prompt.text: What does a failed vision test send you to get?

answer.text: A completed Report of Vision Examination form from an eye doctor.

rationale.text: After a failed vision test, the next step is an eye doctor who completes the vision report form.

narration.text: This lesson begins the testing process with the vision test. DMV vision-tests every applicant to confirm that their sight is adequate for safe driving. That makes the vision test the first check most applicants meet. We will look at what happens if you test while wearing glasses or contact lenses, what happens if you do not pass, and where the full vision standards are written down. These rules are short, but each one has a clear consequence, and knowing them ahead of time means nothing at the counter catches you off guard on the day you apply.

lines.text: Glasses or contacts during the test.

narration.text: If you take the vision test while wearing corrective lenses or contact lenses, the license gets a corrective lenses restriction. In plain terms, the license records that you need those lenses to see well enough for safe driving. This is not a penalty; it is simply a note on your license that matches how you passed. So if you plan to test in your glasses or contacts, expect the restriction to appear. The vision test itself exists to confirm that every applicant's sight is adequate for safe driving, and the restriction is how the license reflects the lenses you rely on.

lines.text: A failed vision test means an eye doctor.
Bring back the vision report form.

narration.text: If you fail the vision test, you are sent to an eye doctor for a completed Report of Vision Examination form. The eye doctor fills out that report, and it becomes part of how DMV judges your eyesight. That is a different path from someone who simply tested in glasses. The lens wearer passed and got a restriction, while the applicant who failed needs the eye doctor's report. If you want to read the standards in full, the DMV keeps a vision standards page that explains them in detail, and that is the best source for questions about your own case.

lines.text: Truth: lenses add a restriction; failing means a referral.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Some applicants think that needing glasses for the vision test means they failed it. That is not right. Testing while wearing corrective or contact lenses puts a corrective lenses restriction on the license, and the applicant still moves forward. Failing is a different outcome: a failed vision test sends you to an eye doctor for a completed Report of Vision Examination form. So lenses lead to a restriction, and failure leads to an eye doctor referral. When a question describes an applicant at the vision test, decide which of those two situations it really describes before you answer.

lines.text: The vision test was not passed.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: an applicant does not pass the vision test. What must they get next? Settle on an answer. The answer is a completed Report of Vision Examination form from an eye doctor. A failed vision test sends you to an eye doctor, who completes that report. If you said the applicant simply gets a corrective lenses restriction, remember that the restriction is for someone who passed while wearing lenses. If you named the eye doctor and the vision report form, you have the two outcomes of the vision test sorted out correctly.

To sum up, DMV vision-tests every applicant to confirm sight adequate for safe driving. If you test while wearing corrective or contact lenses, your license gets a corrective lenses restriction. If you fail the vision test, you go to an eye doctor for a completed Report of Vision Examination form. The detailed vision standards are on the DMV vision standards page. With the vision test covered, the next lesson moves to the knowledge test: its format, how many attempts you get, how long minors wait to retake it, and the rules on testing aids.

why_how.text: Knowing the attempt limit and the retake wait helps you plan when to test.
Bringing a phone or handbook into the test is not allowed, so leaving them aside avoids trouble.

scenario.text: Zoe, a minor, fails her first knowledge test attempt.

reasoning.text: She has three attempts before she must reapply, and as a minor she waits seven days, excluding the failure day, before retaking it.

result.text: Zoe has two attempts left and plans her retake for seven days later, not counting the day she failed.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating eLearning as a testing choice guaranteed to every applicant.

correction.text: The page describes eLearning as a possible renewal testing alternative, with no failing result and quizzes following its modules.

prompt.text: What testing alternative might be offered when a driver renews a license?

answer.text: A no-fail, self-paced eLearning course with quizzes after its modules.

rationale.text: The source says eLearning may be a testing alternative at renewal; that is a possible option, not a guarantee for every applicant.

narration.text: This lesson covers the knowledge test. An original license requires passing a knowledge test built from multiple choice questions. We will look at how many attempts you get, how long a minor must wait after failing, the eLearning option that some renewing drivers may use instead, when your testing options open up, and the strict rule on testing aids. These rules work together, and several of them involve numbers that are easy to confuse with the drive test rules you will meet in the next lesson. Pay close attention to which number belongs to which test.

You get three attempts to pass the knowledge test before you must reapply. If a minor fails, they must wait seven days, excluding the day of the failure, before retaking the knowledge test. Put together, the knowledge test bundles format, attempts, and retakes: multiple choice questions, three tries before reapplying, and a seven-day wait for minors that does not count the failure day. Keep the seven-day number tied to the knowledge test. The drive test has its own, longer wait for minors, and mixing the two is one of the most common errors in this section.

For a renewal, eLearning may be offered as an alternative testing option. It is an interactive course that you work through at your own pace, with a quiz after each module and no failing result. It can run on a computer, laptop, tablet or mobile device. Testing options become available after the application on the DMV driver's license page is completed. Keep the application step separate from the testing choice: finish the application first, then review the options actually offered for that application.

No testing aids are allowed during knowledge tests. That means neither the handbook nor a cell phone may be used while you take the test. Everything you answer has to come from what you have learned. This is why studying the handbook ahead of time matters so much: the knowledge test is built from multiple choice questions on its contents, and you cannot look anything up once it begins. Leave the handbook and your phone aside before you start, so there is no question about whether you followed the rule. The rule is the same for every applicant.

lines.text: Trap: a guaranteed option for all.
Renewal: eLearning may be an option.

narration.text: Here is a trap: treating eLearning as a testing choice guaranteed to every applicant. The page describes it as a possible alternative when renewing a license; it does not make that broad promise. Its useful features are that it is interactive, self-paced and no-fail, with quizzes after its modules. A separate rule concerns minors who fail a knowledge test: they wait seven days, excluding the day of failure, before trying again. Do not transfer that waiting period to a drive test. Read which test and applicant the rule describes.

Here is a quick check: what testing alternative might be offered when a driver renews a license? Think of the answer. The page says eLearning may be an option. It is a self-paced interactive course with quizzes following each module and no failing result. That is the limited claim to remember; do not turn a possible renewal option into a guarantee for all applicants. The same page separately requires an original applicant to pass a multiple-choice knowledge test, allowing three attempts before reapplication. Keep these two source statements distinct.

Let us review. An original license requires a knowledge test built from multiple choice questions. You get three attempts to pass before you must reapply, and minors wait seven days, excluding the failure day, before a retake. Renewing drivers may use eLearning, a no-fail self-paced course with quizzes after each module, but it never replaces the original-license test. Testing options open once your application is complete, and no testing aids, neither the handbook nor a cell phone, are allowed. Next comes the behind-the-wheel test and its own rules.

why_how.text: The drive test grades your driving skill, so knowing how the examiner works helps you stay calm.

scenario.text: During the drive test the examiner tells Ben to turn right at the next corner and then change into the left lane.

reasoning.text: The examiner may stack two or more instructions at once to see whether the driver grasps and follows both.

result.text: Ben listens to both parts and carries out each one safely.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a minor waits the same seven days after failing the drive test.

correction.text: Minors wait fourteen days, excluding the failure day, before retaking a failed behind-the-wheel test.

memory_support.text: Seven for knowledge, fourteen for driving.

prompt.text: How long does a minor wait to retake a failed behind-the-wheel test?

answer.text: Fourteen days, not counting the day of the failure.

rationale.text: The drive test wait for minors is fourteen days, twice the seven-day knowledge test wait.

lines.text: The drive test grades driving skill.
Who takes it and how to book.

narration.text: This lesson is about the behind-the-wheel test, the test that grades how you actually drive. We will look at who must take it, how the examiner may give instructions during it, where to book an appointment, and how long a minor must wait to retake it after a failure. We will also set the three tests of this section side by side, because each one checks something different. Vision screens eyesight, knowledge probes the rules, and the drive test grades your skill behind the wheel. Keeping those purposes straight makes the rest of the section easier.

Original applicants take a behind-the-wheel test of safe driving ability. Renewing drivers who have a vision or medical condition may have to take one too. So the drive test is not only for first-timers. During the test, the examiner may stack two or more instructions at once to see whether you grasp and follow both. That is a deliberate check of your attention and understanding. When you hear more than one instruction, listen for every part and carry each one out safely. Drive-test appointments are booked on the DMV make-an-appointment page.

The three tests in this section gate three different things. The vision test screens your eyesight. The knowledge test probes what you know about the rules. The behind-the-wheel test grades your driving skill. Seeing them side by side helps you place every other rule. Restrictions and eye doctor reports belong to the vision test. Multiple choice questions, three attempts, and the seven-day minor wait belong to the knowledge test. Stacked instructions and the fourteen-day minor wait belong to the drive test. When a question names a rule, ask which of the three tests it belongs to.

lines.text: Trap: seven days after a failed drive test.

narration.text: Here is a trap. After learning that minors wait seven days to retake a failed knowledge test, many learners assume the same seven days applies to the drive test. It does not. Minors wait fourteen days, excluding the day of the failure, before retaking a failed behind-the-wheel test. The knowledge test wait is seven days, and the drive test wait is fourteen. Both waits leave out the failure day itself. When a question mentions a minor who failed a test, first decide which test it was, then pick the matching wait, so the two numbers never trade places.

lines.text: A minor failed the drive test.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: how long does a minor wait to retake a failed behind-the-wheel test? Choose your answer. The answer is fourteen days, not counting the day of the failure. That is twice the seven-day wait that applies after a failed knowledge test. If you said seven days, you borrowed the knowledge test number by mistake, so link fourteen to driving and seven to knowledge. If you said fourteen, you have the two waits sorted out, along with the rule that neither one counts the day the test was failed. Seven goes with knowledge, fourteen with driving.

lines.text: Originals take it; some renewals too.

narration.text: To wrap up, original applicants take a behind-the-wheel test of safe driving ability, and renewing drivers with a vision or medical condition may have to take one too. The examiner may stack two or more instructions to see whether you follow both. Appointments are booked on the DMV make-an-appointment page. Minors wait fourteen days, excluding the failure day, before retaking a failed drive test. Across the section, vision screens eyesight, knowledge probes rules, and the drive test grades skill. Next we look at what you must bring on test day.

title.text: What to bring on test day

why_how.text: Arriving without one required item can mean no test that day.

scenario.text: Sara, a minor with a permit, plans to take her drive test in a rental car with her twenty-five-year-old licensed uncle.

reasoning.text: She must bring her permit, a licensed driver at least twenty-five, and a safe vehicle with insurance and registration; the rental needs her name on the contract with no clause excluding drive tests.

result.text: Sara checks that her name is on the rental contract and that it allows drive tests before test day.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any rental car can be used for the drive test.

correction.text: Rental cars qualify only with your name on the rental contract and no clause excluding drive tests.

prompt.text: A rental car contract has your name on it but excludes drive tests. Can you test in that car?

answer.text: No, the contract must not exclude drive tests.

rationale.text: A rental qualifies only when both conditions hold: your name on the contract and no drive test exclusion.

lines.text: Four kinds of things to bring.
Missing one can stop the test.

narration.text: This lesson covers what you must bring on the day of your drive test. The list falls into four categories: papers for you, a licensed adult beside you, a legal car beneath you, and, if the car is a rental, rental terms that permit testing. Each category has a specific rule, and missing any one of them can keep the test from going ahead. We will go through each item, look at the special conditions for rental cars, and work through an example of a test-day arrival so you can check your own plan against the requirements before the day comes.

lines.text: Bring a licensed driver if needed.

narration.text: On test day, bring your instruction permit or license if you have one. You must also bring another California-licensed driver, unless you are already licensed to drive. That driver must be at least eighteen, or at least twenty-five if you are a minor. These are two separate items: your own papers, and a licensed adult to accompany you. A minor who shows up with an eighteen-year-old licensed friend does not meet the rule, because minors need a companion aged twenty-five or older. Check both items, your document and your companion, before you leave for the test.

lines.text: Rentals need your name, no exclusion.

narration.text: You must bring a vehicle that is safe for the test, along with valid proof of insurance and the vehicle registration. If you use a rental car, it qualifies only when your name is on the rental contract and the contract has no clause excluding drive tests. So a rental adds two conditions on top of the usual vehicle rules. Put the four categories together: your papers, a licensed adult, a legal car with insurance and registration, and rental terms that permit testing. If any category is missing, the test plan is not complete.

lines.text: Truth: your name, and no test exclusion.

narration.text: Here is a trap. People assume that because a rental car is insured and registered, it can always be used for the drive test. The handbook adds two conditions. Your name must be on the rental contract, and the contract must not contain a clause excluding drive tests. If a friend rented the car in their own name, or the contract forbids drive tests, the car does not qualify. Before booking a rental for your test, read the contract and confirm both conditions. The usual vehicle rules still apply as well: the car must be safe and have valid insurance proof and registration.

lines.text: Your name is on the rental.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a rental car contract has your name on it, but it includes a clause excluding drive tests. Can you take the test in that car? Make your choice. The answer is no. A rental qualifies only when both conditions hold: your name is on the contract, and there is no clause excluding drive tests. Having your name on the contract is not enough by itself. If you answered no, you have the rental rule. If not, remember that both conditions must be met, along with the usual safe vehicle, insurance proof, and registration.

To close, on test day bring your instruction permit or license if you have one. Bring another California-licensed driver, at least eighteen, or at least twenty-five for minors, unless you are already licensed. Bring a vehicle safe for the test with valid insurance proof and registration. If it is a rental, your name must be on the contract and the contract must not exclude drive tests. Those are the four categories: papers for you, a licensed adult beside you, a legal car beneath you, and rental terms that permit testing. Next we check the vehicle itself.

why_how.text: A vehicle that fails the check gets the test rescheduled, so a quick walk-around beforehand saves a wasted trip.
The demonstrations show the examiner you can work the vehicle's basic controls.

scenario.text: Kim's car has one mirror on the left and one inside, both brake lights work, and the tires have plenty of tread, but the spare on the back is a donut tire.

reasoning.text: Donut tires are barred from the test, and a vehicle that fails these requirements gets the drive test rescheduled.

result.text: Kim replaces the donut tire with a regular tire before the test, or the test would be rescheduled.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the one-inch rule is about tire tread.

correction.text: One inch is the clearance the pressed foot brake must keep above the floorboard; tread needs at least a thirty-second of an inch.

memory_support.text: Two mirrors, thin tread, inch of pedal, horn heard far.

prompt.text: How much clearance must the pressed foot brake keep above the floorboard?

rationale.text: The brake pedal must keep at least one inch of clearance, separate from the tire tread minimum.

narration.text: Before the drive test begins, the examiner checks your vehicle in a pre-drive inspection. Some items are checked on the car itself, such as the windows, mirrors, lights, tires, brake pedal, and horn. Others are things you must demonstrate, such as the parking brake and arm signals. If the vehicle fails these requirements, the drive test is rescheduled. This lesson walks through every item in order, picks out the numbers you must remember, and separates what the examiner looks at from what you must show. A quick walk-around at home can save you a wasted trip.

lines.text: Two mirrors, one on the left.

narration.text: The pre-drive check starts with a driver window that opens and a windshield giving you and the examiner a full, clear, unblocked view. Cracks in the windshield can postpone the test. Next, the vehicle needs at least two rearview mirrors, and one of them must be on the vehicle's left side. Both the right and the left brake lights must work as well. These items are about seeing and being seen: you need a clear view out, mirrors to watch behind you, and brake lights so drivers behind you know when you slow down. Check all of these before test day.

lines.text: Tread at least a thirty-second inch.
Pedal clearance at least one inch.
Horn heard from two hundred feet.

narration.text: Three more items come with numbers. Tires need at least one thirty-second of an inch of uniform tread depth, and donut tires are barred from the test. When the foot brake is pressed down, it must keep at least one inch of clearance above the floorboard. The horn must be designed for the vehicle, must work, and must be audible from at least two hundred feet away. Put the numbers together: at least two mirrors with one on the left, a thirty-second of an inch of tread, one inch of pedal clearance, and a horn heard at two hundred feet.

lines.text: Set and release the parking brake.

narration.text: Some checks are demonstrations you perform. You must show how to set and release the parking brake. You must demonstrate the left turn, right turn, and slowing-or-stopping arm signals. The wipers may be function-checked, and every seat belt must work and be worn by each occupant. This demonstration trio covers hands, arms, and gear: the parking brake, all three arm signals, and proof that the wipers and belts work. Practice the arm signals before the test so you can show each one without hesitation when the examiner asks.

Here is a worked example. Kim's car has one mirror on the left side and one inside, both brake lights work, and the tires have plenty of tread. But one wheel has a donut tire. Does the car pass the check? Walk through the list. Two mirrors with one on the left, yes. Both brake lights, yes. Tread depth, yes. But donut tires are barred from the test, and a vehicle that fails these requirements gets the drive test rescheduled. Kim needs a regular tire in place of the donut before her test, or she will have to come back another day.

lines.text: Truth: one inch is pedal clearance.

narration.text: Here is a trap built from the numbers. Because the brake pedal rule says one inch, people sometimes attach one inch to the tires. The tire rule is much smaller: at least one thirty-second of an inch of tread depth. One inch is the clearance the pressed foot brake must keep above the floorboard. Another number to keep straight is the horn distance of two hundred feet, and the mirror count of at least two, with one on the left. When a question gives you a number, match it to the right part of the car before you decide whether the vehicle passes.

lines.text: The foot brake is pressed down.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: when the foot brake is pressed all the way down, how much clearance must it keep above the floorboard? Pick your answer. The answer is at least one inch. That number belongs to the brake pedal, not to the tires, which need at least one thirty-second of an inch of tread. If you answered one inch, you have one of the trickiest numbers in the vehicle check. If you mixed it with tread depth, go back over the number cluster: mirrors, tread, pedal clearance, and horn distance, each tied to its own part of the car.

To wrap up the vehicle check: the driver window must open and the windshield must give a full, clear view. You need at least two rearview mirrors with one on the left, and both brake lights must work. Tires need at least a thirty-second of an inch of tread with no donut tires, the pressed brake pedal needs one inch of clearance, and the horn must be heard from two hundred feet. You demonstrate the parking brake, three arm signals, wipers, and belts worn by every occupant. If the vehicle fails, the drive test is rescheduled.

why_how.text: The test grades the driver, so the rules on passengers, recording and vehicle technology all keep the focus on you.

scenario.text: Raj's car has a backup camera and an adaptive cruise control feature, and he speaks through an interpreter.

reasoning.text: Adaptive cruise control is banned, the backup camera is allowed but never replaces direct checks, and the interpreter may help only with controls during the pre-drive inspection.

result.text: Raj turns off adaptive cruise control, still checks his mirrors and blind spots himself, and his interpreter stays behind once the drive begins.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a backup camera replaces looking over your shoulder.

correction.text: Safety tech such as backup cameras is allowed yet never replaces direct mirror and blind-spot checks.

memory_support.text: Helpers banned, viewers allowed, your eyes always.

prompt.text: Is adaptive cruise control allowed during the drive test?

answer.text: No, assistance technology like adaptive cruise control is banned.

rationale.text: The test grades the driver rather than the car, so tech that drives for you is not allowed.

lines.text: What devices and tech are allowed.

narration.text: This lesson covers the rules that apply while the drive test is under way. The test grades the driver rather than the car, and that idea explains most of these rules. We will look at who may ride along, how far an interpreter may help, the ban on recording devices, and which vehicle technologies are banned or allowed. We will finish with where to find sample score sheets so you can see how driving is evaluated. Knowing these rules ahead of time means no surprises at the start of the test and no last-minute scramble to change your setup.

lines.text: Interpreters stop at the pre-drive check.

narration.text: Only the examiner accompanies the drive test, except for training, service animals, and certain law enforcement situations. Interpreters may help you identify and use the vehicle controls during the pre-drive inspection, but they cannot ride along for the test itself. So an interpreter's role ends once the inspection is done. Parents, friends, and interpreters do not ride along; the examiner does. If you rely on an interpreter, use that help during the inspection to make sure you understand the controls, because once the drive begins, it is you and the examiner in the car.

lines.text: Block any that cannot power off.

narration.text: Recording devices, including video recorders, are prohibited on the drive test. If a device cannot be powered off, it must be blocked from all visual and audio recording. That covers phones and dashboard cameras alike. Put the conduct rules together and you get a simple picture: only the examiner rides along, interpreters stop at the pre-drive inspection, and every recorder stays off or blocked. Before the test, check your vehicle for anything that records, and either switch it off or block it so it cannot capture any video or sound during the drive.

Because the test grades the driver rather than the car, assistance technology is banned. That includes automated parallel parking, lane departure features, and adaptive cruise control. Safety technology such as backup cameras and blind spot monitors is allowed, yet it never replaces your own direct mirror and blind-spot checks. The line is simple: technology that drives for you is banned, while technology that only shows you more is allowed but cannot do your looking for you. Sample Driving Performance Evaluation Score Sheets are on the DMV teen driver page, with Supplemental and Area sheets on the seniors page.

lines.text: Trap: the camera replaces head checks.
Truth: you still check mirrors and blind spots.

narration.text: Here is a trap. Because backup cameras and blind spot monitors are allowed on the drive test, some drivers lean on them and skip turning their heads. That is a mistake. Safety technology is allowed, but it never replaces direct mirror and blind-spot checks. You still have to look for yourself. A second trap is the opposite: assuming any helpful feature is fine. Assistance features such as automated parallel parking, lane departure, and adaptive cruise control are banned, because the test grades your driving rather than the car's. Use allowed tech, but keep doing every check yourself.

lines.text: The car has adaptive cruise control.
Is it allowed on the test?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: is adaptive cruise control allowed during the drive test? Make your call. The answer is no. Adaptive cruise control is assistance technology, and assistance technology is banned because the test grades the driver rather than the car. A backup camera or blind spot monitor would be allowed, but even those never replace your own mirror and blind-spot checks. If you said no, you have the line between banned and allowed technology. If you said yes, remember the rule that features which drive for you are not permitted on the test.

To sum up, only the examiner accompanies the drive test, except for training, service animals, and certain law enforcement situations. Interpreters may help with controls during the pre-drive inspection but cannot ride along. Recording devices are prohibited, and any that cannot be powered off must be blocked. Assistance technology is banned because the test grades the driver, while safety technology is allowed yet never replaces your own checks. Sample score sheets are on the DMV teen driver and seniors pages. That completes the testing process.
